*Artigo 30.º-B*
*Âmbito objectivo*
1 - Estão abrangidas pelo âmbito de aplicação do SDR as +embalagens primárias não reutilizáveis de bebidas em plástico, metais ferrosos e alumínio com uma volumetria inferior a 3 litros, que sejam colocadas no mercado devidamente marcadas, após a data de entrada em funcionamento operacional do sistema de depósito e reembolso.+
2 - Para efeitos do disposto no número anterior +consideram-se as seguintes categorias de bebidas:+
a) Águas minerais e de nascente e outras águas embaladas;
b) Sumos e néctares, e mixes de frutas e vegetais;
c) Concentrados para diluição;
d) Refrigerantes, incluindo bebidas à base de chá, café e tisanas;
e) Bebidas energéticas e isotónicas;
f) Cerveja, sidra, sangria e mixes alcoólicos.
3 - +São excluídas+ do âmbito do SDR +as embalagens de serviço e as embalagens primárias de bebidas que contenham mais de 25 /prct. de ingredientes de origem láctea+.
4 - São ainda excluídas do âmbito de aplicação do SDR as embalagens referidas nos n.os 1 e 2 que, por motivos excecionais e devidamente fundamentados, não apresentem características compatíveis com o sistema de depósito e reembolso de acordo com o disposto no n.º 1 do artigo 30.º-L.
5 - Para efeitos do número anterior, a APA, I. P., e a DGAE podem solicitar esclarecimentos adicionais ao requerente da exclusão.

*Artigo 30.º-E*
*Determinação e cobrança do valor de depósito*
1 - +É cobrado ao consumidor final um valor de depósito por cada embalagem abrangida pelo sistema, recuperável mediante o retorno da embalagem usada, em locais especificamente destinados a esse efeito.+
2 - O valor de depósito é determinado por despacho dos membros do Governo responsáveis pelas áreas da economia e do ambiente, podendo ser revisto por sua iniciativa ou sob proposta devidamente fundamentada das entidades gestoras do SDR, designadamente quando não se encontre assegurado o cumprimento da meta de recolha, acompanhada de estudos de mercado e de consumidor.
3 - O valor de depósito a fixar nos termos do número anterior não está sujeito a tributação, devendo estimular a devolução da embalagem usada.
4 - As entidades gestoras do SDR cobram aos embaladores aderentes o valor de depósito por cada embalagem de bebida colocada no mercado.
5 - +O valor de depósito é transmitido ao longo de toda a cadeia de distribuição, desde a colocação no mercado até ao consumidor final, devendo ser discriminado em todas as faturas e identificado nos suportes utilizados para a indicação do preço do produto.+
6 - O +valor de depósito é cobrado ao consumidor final no ato da venda de bebidas, independentemente da técnica de venda utilizada, incluindo por via eletrónica ou à distância+, com exceção dos casos previstos no artigo 30.º-I para os estabelecimentos do setor HORECA.

*Artigo 30.º-F*
*Reembolso do valor de depósito*
1 - +O reembolso do valor de depósito+ ao consumidor final +pode ser realizado por uma das seguintes formas:+
a) No caso dos pontos de recolha manuais, em numerário ou através de outras modalidades, designadamente, troca por troca ou vale de compras no exato valor do depósito;
b) No caso dos pontos de recolha automática, através de formas de pagamento desmaterializadas, donativos ou mediante a emissão de um vale comprovativo do retorno que pode ser redimido em numerário ou através de outras modalidades, designadamente, vale de compras, ou atividades e serviços que correspondam ao exato valor do depósito.
2 - A opção pelo reembolso em numerário não pode ser retirada ou condicionada.
3 - Os responsáveis pelos pontos de recolha referidos nos artigos 30.º-G e 30.º-H, bem como pelos estabelecimentos do setor HORECA referidos no artigo 30.º-I devem reembolsar de imediato os consumidores finais que pretendam receber o valor de depósito, mediante a entrega das embalagens ou dos vales emitidos nas máquinas de recolha automática, conforme aplicável.
4 - Excetuam-se do disposto nos números anteriores as situações em que existam dúvidas fundadas quanto à autenticidade ou regularidade do vale apresentado, casos em que pode ser recusado o reembolso do valor de depósito.
5 - As entidades gestoras do SDR podem determinar um prazo de validade para os vales previstos na alínea b) do n.º 1, o qual não pode ser inferior a 12 meses.
6 - O prazo de pagamento dos valores de depósito pelas entidades gestoras do SDR aos responsáveis pelos pontos de recolha referidos no artigo 30.º-H e estabelecimentos do setor HORECA referidos no artigo 30.º-I não pode ser superior a 30 dias seguidos, contados a partir da data de entrega dos resíduos de embalagens pelos referidos estabelecimentos nos centros de consolidação ou de triagem e contagem das entidades gestoras do SDR.
7 - Não são sujeitas a reembolso as embalagens que se encontrem danificadas ou com rótulo ilegível de modo a impedir a correta identificação, nos termos a definir nas licenças do SDR.

 *Artigo 30.º-G*
*Rede de pontos de recolha*
1 - A rede de pontos de recolha é estruturada nos termos a fixar nas licenças das entidades gestoras do SDR, constituindo-se a partir da conjugação de:
a) Estabelecimentos de comércio a retalho, nos termos do disposto no n.º 1 do artigo seguinte;
b) Pontos de recolha definidos em resultado de acordos celebrados, nomeadamente, com estabelecimentos do setor HORECA, com os municípios ou com os sistemas municipais e multimunicipais de gestão de resíduos urbanos;
c) Outros pontos de recolha instalados em espaço público e em espaços municipais, por iniciativa e responsabilidade das entidades gestoras do SDR.
2 - A instalação da rede de pontos de recolha nos casos previstos na alínea c) do número anterior carece de autorização da entidade responsável pela gestão de resíduos na respetiva área de recolha, nos termos da legislação aplicável aos serviços municipais de abastecimento público de água, saneamento e resíduos urbanos e à concessão da exploração e gestão dos sistemas multimunicipais de tratamento e de recolha seletiva de resíduos urbanos, e de acordo com os contratos de concessão respetivos, quando existam.
3 - A recolha dos resíduos de embalagens nos pontos de recolha nos casos previstos na alínea c) do n.º 1 deve ser realizada com uma periodicidade a acordar entre as entidades gestoras do SDR e o responsável pelo ponto de recolha, em articulação com os sistemas municipais e multimunicipais de gestão de resíduos urbanos quando realizem a recolha a partir dos pontos de recolha.
4 - A instalação de pontos de recolha deve ser precedida de contratos escritos a celebrar entre as entidades gestoras do SDR e a entidade responsável pelo ponto de recolha de acordo com a minuta definida pela APA, I. P.
5 - Para efeitos do disposto no n.º 2, a decisão sobre o pedido de autorização deve ser proferida no prazo de 60 dias consecutivos desde a data da sua apresentação.
6 - Decorrido o prazo referido no número anterior sem que a decisão tenha sido proferida e comunicada às entidades gestoras do SDR, considera-se autorizada a instalação dos pontos de recolha.



Artigo 30.º-H
Pontos de recolha nos estabelecimentos de comércio a retalho
1 - Nos estabelecimentos de comércio a retalho onde se comercializem bebidas cujas embalagens integram o SDR é obrigatória a receção dos resíduos de embalagens mediante a instalação de pontos de recolha, nos seguintes termos:
a) Estabelecimentos com área de exposição e venda contínua igual ou superior a 400 m2, com a obrigação de receber todas as embalagens incluídas no SDR;
b) Estabelecimentos com área de exposição e venda contínua superior a 50 m2 e inferior a 400 m2, com a obrigação de receber apenas as embalagens de bebidas que vendam no seu estabelecimento, sem prejuízo do disposto no número seguinte.
2 - Os estabelecimentos a que se refere a alínea b) do número anterior que apresentem comprovada falta de condições para a receção de embalagens ficam dispensados do cumprimento da obrigação prevista no n.º 1, desde que exista uma densidade mínima suficiente de pontos de recolha no local em que se situam.
3 - Os estabelecimentos a que se refere a alínea b) do n.º 1, que optem por se constituir como ponto de recolha automático estão obrigados a aceitar todas as embalagens de bebidas que integram o SDR, sem prejuízo de poderem optar por receber as embalagens que não comercializem no caso de se constituírem como pontos de recolha manuais.
4 - Os estabelecimentos com área de exposição e venda contínua igual ou inferior a 50 m2 e os que, independentemente da área de exposição e venda contínua, tenham uma atividade de comércio de produtos alimentares que represente menos de 10 /prct. do respetivo volume total de vendas, estão isentos da obrigação de recolha dos resíduos de embalagens, podendo optar por constituir-se como ponto de recolha mediante acordo com as entidades gestoras do SDR.
5 - A opção pelo caráter automático ou manual da recolha cabe ao responsável pelo ponto de recolha, cabendo às entidades gestoras do SDR definir as especificações técnicas a que devem obedecer os equipamentos de recolha automática de modo a assegurar a sua compatibilidade com o SDR.

Artigo 30.º-U
Marcação das embalagens
1 - As embalagens devem ser marcadas através de um símbolo de inclusão no SDR e de um código EAN.
2 - O símbolo mencionado no número anterior, bem como as regras para a sua aposição, são definidos pela APA, I. P., e DGAE, mediante proposta das entidades gestoras do SDR.
3 - A APA, I. P., e a DGAE aprovam e publicitam as regras de elegibilidade para a marcação das embalagens com o código EAN a que se refere o n.º 1, mediante propostas das entidades gestoras do SDR.
4 - As marcações referidas no n.º 1 podem ser apostas por impressão direta ou rotulagem.



Artigo 30.º-V
Obrigações dos embaladores
Sem prejuízo de outros deveres que resultem do presente regime, são obrigações dos embaladores aderentes às entidades gestoras do SDR:
a) Marcar as embalagens nos termos previstos no artigo anterior;
b) Submeter as embalagens à aprovação prévia das entidades gestoras do SDR, fornecendo toda a informação necessária;
c) Efetuar o pagamento da prestação financeira e do valor de depósito às entidades gestoras do SDR por cada embalagem colocada no mercado;
d) Cobrar o valor de depósito por cada embalagem colocada no mercado;
e) Discriminar o valor de depósito nas faturas de venda;
f) Colaborar com as entidades gestoras do SDR na divulgação das campanhas de sensibilização, comunicação e educação dirigidas aos consumidores finais e aos demais intervenientes no SDR;
g) Colaborar nas auditorias previstas na alínea n) do n.º 1 do artigo 12.º, prestando a informação e os esclarecimentos que lhe forem solicitados.

Hi [~accountid:712020:822a759a-daf0-4161-afbf-8b79a2985fba] , given that users will still be able to use the funds they’ve already deposited, there is no specific minimum notification period under Dutch law for discontinuing the top-up functionality. PSD2 notification requirements don’t apply since we have the exclusion. Our T&Cs also don’t require any specific notification period for this change. 

But, under general principles of transparency and fairness in Dutch consumer protection law, users should be informed in advance of any material change to the functionality they use. So even though the T&Cs already allow for the top-up feature to be unavailable in certain countries, providing prior notice would be the most transparent and customer-friendly approach. The notification period that would most closely align with user expectations (and therefore transparency and fairness principles) would likely be the one-month notice period required for full service termination under the T&Cs.

Hi [~accountid:712020:822a759a-daf0-4161-afbf-8b79a2985fba] , essentially the same applies here as for the NL. 

The Swiss T&Cs don’t specify a minimum period for this type of change. Swiss consumer protection law does not prescribe a specific notice period for the switch-off either, but generally users must be treated fairly and be informed in advance of a change that affects how they can use the product. So best practice would be to give reasonable advance notice so they aren’t caught off guard or disadvantaged. As is the case in the NL, the notice period that would most closely align with user expectations would be 1 month, as that is the notice period for terminating the service.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Marten

Ok, the issue is simple, but not displayed in an understandable way. It’s about the selection in the dbt command.

Current definition:

{noformat}dbt build --select tag:fact_vehicle_registration tag:fact_vehicle_registration_submissions{noformat}

The {{tag:fact_vehicle_registration_submissions}} is passed as an argument to dbt, and not a part of select. 

It either should be enclosed with quotes as described here [https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/node-selection/set-operators|https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/node-selection/set-operators|smart-link] or add a second {{--select}}:

{noformat}--select tag:fact_vehicle_registration --select tag:fact_vehicle_registration_submissions{noformat}

Questions to external counsel:

We are reviewing the compliance of our age verification process under the Colorado Privacy Act (CPA) and the recent HB24-1130 amendments.

Our current flow involves:

* A *selfie age verification* step, where we process a user’s facial measurements to estimate age;
* If the user does *not consent* to selfie processing, we offer *automated document verification* (automated extraction of date of birth from an uploaded ID); and
* If the user does not consent to automated verification, they can proceed with *manual document verification* performed by a member of our operations team.

In this context, could you please advise on the following:

* *Legal requirements for processing biometric data* under the CPA and HB24-1130 (or any other relevant laws).
* Whether our current *consent screen* is likely to meet the CPA’s standards for valid consent (see attached).
* Whether any additional disclosures to our *Privacy Notice disclosures* ('_To authenticate your account and verify your identity_' [section|https://gethopp.com/en-us/privacy/privacy-for-micromobility/?category=micromobility]) are necessary for biometric processing.

We would appreciate your confirmation on whether the current flow aligns with Colorado’s biometric data requirements, or if adjustments are needed to ensure full compliance.

Hi [@leandro.morgado|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U01AH7VKNHY], we did some investigation and I would like to present you the findings. Let's take per example the execution plan from above; we have tikv_wall_time = 255.4 ms and total_time = 926.5 ms. We have total_keys = 500 and total_process_keys = 500, which means that MVCC amp ratio is 1(process_keys/total_keys) and leads to the conclusion that IME is not helping here since that default is 10. We see here num_rpc = 17 which means that we have 17 batch_point_get requests sent to tikv. The longest cost is 255.4, which implies that the rest of aprox. ~750ms is being spent by the 17 request scheduling. If we check tikv details metrics, we see that P999 of kv batch_get reaches 300~500ms that matches period when you notice this kind of behavior. The unified read pool metrics doesn't show constant pressure on thread pool, so this means that this short term long latency that you are seeing comes from other big request that  holds threads for too long. The reason why i'm asking how many occurrences you see in slow query logs is to do a rough ratio between total executions and   number of executions for more than 300 ms to understand the percentage. In our case per. example  you have more or less 11k total executions and maybe 30-40 occurrences of executions with more than 300 ms, which give us a percentage of aprox. 0.002. Although, if you check the print-screen we can see that spikes in ms on gRPC message duration happens on P999 and this for all queries that use batch_get, so it must be below 0.1%. In this case and based on discussion with our colleagues from product group, seems to be expected behavior since that for a very short period, if you have increased workload in terms of requests that keep hold on threads for longer time, this query(and other) might wait for an available thread to be available for finalizing execution. As as solution, it will be either to scale tivk, use resource control or work on query optimization for slow queries and reduce the execution time that implicit, will reduce the probability of this issue to occur. One more thing, i've analyzed multiple executions of the query, from 300-400 ms to 900 ms and what i see as pattern, tikv_wall_time move between 250-300 ms for all of them, which means that the delay comes from short term busy threads. Please, let us know about any additional information you might have.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* On 27 October, we received an email from a Ukrainian lawyer ([link|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/674414302]) requesting information relating to an accident that their client (Yuliya Kostetska) was in.
** Accident occurred on 3 May 2024 at approximately 15:50 in Kyiv.
* Lawyer has requested the following:
** 1. Information about the passenger in the car with licence plate КА5042КН (driven by Vyacheslav Ihorovych Revnivtsev) involved in the accident, in particular: Name and phone number.
** 2. Information on whether the driver Vyacheslav Ihorovych Revnivtsev was (on 3 May 2024), and still is, working for Bolt (“_in a civil-law relationship regarding the fulfillment of orders in the interests of passengers and/or BOLT OPERATIONS UKRAINE LLC and/or with Bolt Operations OÜ_”).
** 3. Copy of the agreement between Vyacheslav Ihorovych Revnivtsev and Bolt on 3 May 2024.
** 4. Copy of the document “_confirming the legal grounds for Vyacheslav Ihorovych Revnivtsev to display and advertise_” the Bolt brand on his car on 3 May 2024.
** 5. Information on whether Vyacheslav Ihorovych Revnivtsev is registered as a “Private Entrepreneur” as a Bolt driver.
** 6. Copy of the following relating to the driver’s car: (i) “_the liability insurance contract for damage caused to the life and health of passengers while using the transport_”; and (ii) “_the compulsory civil liability insurance contract for damage caused to the life, health, and property of third parties_”.
** 7. Information on whether Yaroslav Stanislavovych Hrushkevych (the owner of the car with licence plate КА5042КН) was (on 3 May 2024), and still is, working for Bolt (“_in a civil-law relationship regarding the fulfillment of orders in the interests of passengers_”).
** 8. Copy of the agreement between Yaroslav Stanislavovych Hrushkevych and Bolt, governing use of the Bolt brand on the car.
** 9. Copy of the document “_confirming the legal grounds for Yaroslav Stanislavovych Hrushkevych to display and advertise_” the Bolt brand on his car on 3 May 2024.
** 10. Information on whether Yaroslav Stanislavovych Hrushkevych is registered as a “Private Entrepreneur” as a Bolt driver.
* Lawyer has set a deadline of 29 October (which is great for them, but not mandatory as far as I am aware).
** If we fail to comply, “_a relevant statement the commission of a criminal offense under Article 397 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (Interference with the activities of a defender or representative of a person) will be sent to the appropriate law enforcement authorities_”.
* On 28 October, CS (thankfully) responded “_We confirm that we have received your request… Additional time may be required to identify and locate the requested personal data and to assess the necessity, proportionality and legality of your request. We will respond to your request as soon as possible_”.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* *Validity* / *Authority*: ✅ 
** Yurchenko Yuriy & Partners appear to be a legitimate law firm, specialising in dispute resolution. The letter is also signed with an official stamp (and attaches a certificate to practice law), so it appears legitimate.
** Letter attaches an ‘Advocate’s Warrant' (apparently this is a document showing authority to provide legal services - likely akin to a PoA).
* *Legal Basis*: (?) 
** Lawyer has cited “_Articles 20, 23, and 24 of the Law of Ukraine «On the Bar and Advocacy»_” - These do not appear to explicitly _require_ Bolt to share data, although this is worth double-checking with Regional Legal.
*** 20: Right of an advocate to represent a client in legal matters (including requesting documents / evidence).
*** 23: Lists specific safeguards provided to advocates (e.g., confidentiality, independence, immunity from some forms of +_interference_+).
*** 24: Right of advocates to submit requests for information that will assist their client. It is prohibited to request any documents from the advocate other than practicing certificate and authority letter. The entity requested must respond within 5 business days (or up to 20 days in complex cases), otherwise liability applies ⚠️ 
** Only other law cited is Article 397, which criminalises “_interference_” with a legal representative’s activities (e.g., obstructing arrival to court, or hampering access to evidence). A fine or “restriction of liberty” for up to 3 years.
*** IMO this seems like a “scare tactic” more than anything else - provided that Bolt is following its usual data sharing procedures, it is not illegally obstructing this lawyer by asking questions / doing due diligence before sharing any data.
*** Nevertheless, worth checking with Regional Legal whether the usual expectation is to treat this as a mandatory request.
** NB. These laws are not listed in [this spreadsheet|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/19F9dMxdObEnLmTW4PazyKso7fM5c7SSkUwPsON2X1Ow/edit?gid=0#gid=0]. 
*** Also, since Ukraine is outside of the EU (and assuming the disclosing Bolt entity is in Estonia), this would comprise an international transfer of data. We can rely on the derogation in Article 49(1)(e) GDPR (legal claims) to get around the requirement for SCCs, if needed (although this adds further weight to the argument that the data being transferred must be _proportionate_).
* *Proportionality*: ❌ 
** A few elements of this request seem disproportionate:
*** Unclear why the lawyer needs details about the passenger - this seems disproportionate. Could be for witness purposes, but the advocate should specify. Also, email would be less intrusive than phone number.
*** Unclear why the lawyer needs copy of contracts with Bolt (particularly advertising / branding agreements), where this concerns a traffic accident. Confirming that the driver is driving for Bolt should be sufficient.
*** Liability / insurance contracts makes sense I suppose, provided it does not contain any sensitive data.
*** Unclear why the lawyer needs the {color:#ff5630}car owner’s information{color}.
** If we do provide data here, IMO we should provide passenger name and email, confirmation of driver status, any public-facing T&Cs, limited liability insurance information. I do not see how Hrushkevych is relevant here - we should question this.

h3. *Updates Made to Data Protection Provisions*

Following the privacy review, [Section |https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ByknN_LoRMj0x6ONFGxLBNaAsm3MHcYh/edit][*11.16*|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ByknN_LoRMj0x6ONFGxLBNaAsm3MHcYh/edit] *(Medical Confidentiality and Data Protection)* has been *updated* to clarify the roles and responsibilities of both parties and to align with the *Kenyan Data Protection Act, 2019 (KDPA)*. A short comment added to clause 11.16 to explain the provisions added by privacy team.

*Detailed summary of key improvements - for audit trail:*

* ✅ *Independent Controller Relationship* – It is now expressly stated that [http://rescue.co|http://rescue.co]  *and Bolt Support KE Ltd (the Customer)* act as *independent data controllers*.
* ✅ *Limited Data Sharing by Bolt* – Bolt only provides *the name and contact phone number* of the individual in danger when the SOS button is triggered, strictly for the *purpose of enabling* [http://rescue.co|http://rescue.co]  *to coordinate the emergency response*.
* ✅ [http://Rescue.co|http://Rescue.co] *’s Independent Processing* – Any additional or sensitive (medical/health) data collected from the individual is handled *directly and independently by* [http://rescue.co|http://rescue.co] , which bears full responsibility for compliance with the KDPA.
* ✅ *Cooperation Obligations* – Added a short operational clause ensuring:
** mutual notice and cooperation in case of *personal data breaches*;
** coordination on *data subject rights requests*, directing requests to the appropriate controller;
** reasonable cooperation on *authority inquiries or investigations*, and other obligations such as DPIAs;
** confirmation that *each party maintains its own records* and audit trail to demonstrate compliance.
* ✅ [http://Rescue.co|http://Rescue.co] *’s Responsibility for Sub-providers* – Confirmed that [http://rescue.co|http://rescue.co]  remains responsible for ensuring its *third-party emergency or security providers* comply with confidentiality and data protection obligations under the KDPA.
* ✅ *Addition on Data Retention Period*
** the clause will now also include an explicit data retention limitation to ensure applicable to personal data provided by Bolt.
** period - 30 days post-closure of each incident or case, after which [rescue.co|http://rescue.co] must delete or anonymise the personal data, unless retention is required by law or for legitimate record-keeping (e.g., regulatory or insurance-related obligations).
These changes ensure the relationship is properly framed as *controller-to-controller*, with clear accountability and no transfer of compliance responsibility between the parties.

h3. *Alignment with Legal’s Liability and Indemnity Position*

The privacy team confirms alignment with the legal team’s current position on *liability and indemnity* provisions. Specifically:

* *Data protection and confidentiality breaches* are *explicitly carved out* from the general liability limitation clause — meaning [http://Rescue.co|http://Rescue.co] ’s liability for such breaches is *not capped*.
* [http://Rescue.co|http://Rescue.co]  *indemnifies Bolt* for any third-party claims, losses, or damages arising from its negligence, willful misconduct, or breach of data protection, confidentiality, or intellectual property obligations.
* This indemnity provides coverage for *third-party and regulatory claims*.

hey all, getting back with a clarification to align on third-party marketing under Bolt Rewards and to avoid extra or duplicate consents

*_tl;dr:_* We do not move consent into T&Cs and we do not need to ask for multiple consents if the purpose is third-party partner marketing under Bolt Rewards. If a driver has the third-party marketing toggle on in the driver app - we can market partner offers to them. If driver is opted-out (toggle off) we can contact the driver to ask for consent, record their choice, and proceed only if they say yes. We must always honour their preference and may re-ask at reasonable intervals without being intrusive.

+*What this means for the current Romania flow*+

# Bolt Rewards framework
• source of truth - the setting _third_party_marketing_ in the Driver app
• if enabled - we can send partner promotions via the planned channels and you can share the minimal contact data needed with the partner for fulfilment, as per our Rewards setup
• if disabled or not set - we may call or message once with a short consent ask. if they say yes - mark consent and proceed with the offer in the same call. if they say no - mark no-contact and stop. We shall keep an audit trail either way
# No consent via T&Cs, as adding a clause to T&Cs that lets partners contact all drivers is not valid consent. 
# One call is fine, if sequenced correctly
• merge the consent ask and the offer in a single call, but take consent first
example script
_“we’re calling about Bolt Rewards partner offers. do you want to receive these and for us to share your name and phone number with our partners for this purpose”_
if yes → proceed with the offer details
if no → say thank you, mark as no-contact, and end the call
# Preference management and frequency
• record every yes or no in the same system that feeds the app setting, so channels stay in sync
• you can re-ask occasionally to confirm interest, but be mindful of frequency and avoid pressure tactics. if a driver objects through CS, we shall stop contacting them
# Branding and disclosure on calls
• we or the partner can introduce the call as part of the Bolt Rewards programme. if a driver asks who the partner is or how we got their details, we should be transparent and answer plainly. this protects us on transparency

+*how this relates to the past Eternis setup*+

Eternis had a bespoke consent script because the relationship and data flows were special. That does not change the general Bolt Rewards rule above. For standard Rewards partnerships, use the single third-party marketing consent.

+*what we can do:*+

* confirm the single source of truth field is third_party_marketing
* implement the one-call flow with the consent ask first, then offer
* log consent and denials with timestamp, channel, and script version
* suppress outreach across all channels for denials and objections

+*risks if we deviate*+

* T&Cs-based “consent” will not hold and increases enforcement risk
* repeated asks or ignoring a no will lead to complaints and could escalate beyond RO

So we agreed that there are 2 problems:

1. Case may be assigned to an agent while we already assigned it to a system bot for offering disruption comms
2. Case is re-opened while solved as the agent assignment is removed

What we considered

1. Rejecting the assignment from Beehive at the time we know that the case is assigned to the restricted queue and marked as solved with disruption comms offered - but rejecting would mean MQ event processing failure, so the best we could do is ignoring, which would have repercussions (if there’s ever a case where we want some agents to be given access to this queue, even if only for removing the tickets stuck there, it wouldn’t be possible)

2. Ensuring that the case isn’t re-opened when solved upon agent unassignment - that would work as long as offering disruption comms is successful (considering issue #1 described above), but then the case wouldn’t be assigned to a system bot when offering SSAT, which would produce alerts - so that’s not ideal

3. Ideally, upon receiving assignee updated event from Beehive, even though the disruption comms message might have been posted, we should withdraw from the process of offering the disruption comms and remove it from the restricted queue - that could be done in the assinee updated event reducer and probably is the best course of action

Considering that this hasn’t happened for the past 4 months (after we started assigning the support case to bot while offering comms), we may also choose to park it for now to see if this race condition ever re-occurs again.

“Hi [~accountid:62ff8d58b582d07a14a96588], I hope you are well. I have picked this ticket up from Catherine/Ieva and have now looked further into your question of whether Bolt can introduce an activation bonus for new London drivers. My review is set out below:

+1️⃣+ +*Can Bolt run a London-only activation bonus?*+

Yes — there is no legal or regulatory blocker for Bolt testing a small-scale activation incentive in London (for example, “£200 for 200 trips in your first month”). However, the way it is *structured and described* matters because of the different legal risks under Bolt’s two UK operating models.

+2️⃣+ +*How to structure it*+

* The safest route is to treat the bonus as a *discretionary marketing promotion*, not as guaranteed pay. 
* The bonus wording, driver communications and terms must all make clear that it is *non-contractual* and can be withdrawn at Bolt’s discretion.
* The payment can go into the driver’s *in-app balance* and then flow through the normal payout cycle.
* Keep the scheme small and capped (for example, first 100 drivers) to show that it is a test campaign, not an ongoing pay component.

+3️⃣+ +*Treatment under each model*+

Under the *Bolt Standard (Principal) model*, which applies in London, drivers are legally classed as “workers.” This means any trip-linked payment counts as part of their earnings. If you run a London activation bonus under this model, it must therefore be processed through normal pay, included in minimum-wage calculations and pension (auto-enrolment) contributions. You can still run the test, but it sits inside the worker-pay framework rather than as an external marketing incentive.

Under the *Bolt Flex (Agency) model*, used outside London, drivers are independent contractors and Bolt acts only as their agent taking commission. In this setting, an activation bonus can be treated as *marketing spend*, but it must not be used — or appear to be used — to encourage drivers who are eligible for auto-enrolment (i.e., in the Standard model) to opt-out and move to the Flex model. That would risk being seen as an “inducement” under pensions law, which can attract penalties of up to £50,000 per case. Therefore:

* The activation bonus can be funded as a marketing promotion;
* But it must not be linked to, or contingent on, switching models or opting out of pension contributions; and
* All communications about the scheme must be clearly separate from AE or worker-status messaging.

+4️⃣+ +*Operational safeguards for a compliant London pilot*+

* Target *new-to-Bolt* drivers only, not reactivated accounts.
* Do not link the bonus to acceptance rates, minimum hours or driver-score thresholds.
* Use a simple, objective trip-count criterion.
* Make all rules transparent and include standard fraud and fair-use language in the promotional terms.

+✅+ +*In summary*+

Bolt can run a London activation bonus pilot in 2025 if it is:

* Treated as *discretionary marketing spend* rather than contractual pay;
* *Clearly communicated* as a limited promotion; and
* *Compliant* with wage and pension obligations under the Standard model, while not being used to divert auto-enrolment-eligible drivers under the Flex model.

Unless [~accountid:5e2af09cc55f580c9fca70a7], thinks otherwise, I believe we can proceed with introducing the activation bonus scheme for new London drivers in 2025 :green-check:

* Ideally, having all drivers sign the new contract would be fantastic, however recalling a situation at the beginning of the year, we have thousands of drivers that kept performing in accordance with the contract but who had not accepted the new udpated contract. To remedy this, we emailed the drivers to inform them of the update (again) and stipulated that by sending the picture to get paid, this would be considered as acceptance of the new terms.

NJSC {{AwsSqsMqSubscriber}} already supports delaying a message for a number of seconds through {{awsChangeMessageVisibilityBatch}}. The only problem is that there’s no way for the handler to explicitly delay the message: it can succeed or it can fail with an exception.

To support this, we would have to modify the handler as suggested in the description and propagate it to {{batchHandlingSkipped}} with a non-zero delay. Probably would require some refactoring as the delay would be per message, not for the entire batch.

The feature is doable and useful.

👋 Hey there!
If you need a *report*, please refer to FleetX (DriverX). If your request concerns an *invoice*, follow these steps:

1. Open the **Client page in Admin**: [link|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients?tz=Europe%2FTallinn&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D].
2. Enter the Fleet or Driver ID in the **External ID** filter field.
3. Open the driver or fleet profile.
4. Go to the **Invoice tasks** tab.
   * If you see *Invoice sum too small*, no commission invoice was generated because the driver either owed no commission or had more compensation than commission.
   * If you encounter any other error, please let us know.
5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under **Invoice tasks** or **Partner Invoices**.

Best regards,

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Continuing this projects movement forward, altough after SPRK meeting we learned that everything is no so easy as firstly thought and while waiting central teams further comments from other country experiences on similar issues (eta ~1st November week) 

In meantime could we explore option for Bolt to provide “Bolt Send“ category as not postal service but more like transfer service? After quick research and consultation with ChatGPT here is description on how potentially it could work - 


 *1. Juridiskais pamats*

Saskaņā ar *Pasta likuma 1. pantu*, _pasta pakalpojums_ ir komerciāla darbība, kas ietver *adresētu sūtījumu* savākšanu, šķirošanu, pārvadāšanu un piegādi adresātam.
Tādēļ, lai pakalpojums *netiktu kvalificēts kā pasta komercdarbība*, tam *nedrīkst izpildīties šie trīs elementi vienlaikus*:

# Ir *adresēts sūtījums* konkrētai personai (adresātam);
# Pastāv *pasta līgums* starp sūtītāju un komersantu;
# Pakalpojums ietver *sūtījuma piegādi adresātam* ar saņemšanas apstiprinājumu.

----

h3. *2. Kā to formulēt legāli kā transporta pakalpojumu*

“Bolt Send” var pamatot kā *nelielu priekšmetu pārvadājumu starp diviem punktiem*, nevis “pasta sūtījuma piegādi”, ja tiek ievēroti šie principi:

* *Terminoloģija:* izmantot “pārvadājums”, “priekšmets”, “paka”, “punkts A–B”, nevis “sūtījums”, “adresāts”, “piegāde”.
* *Līguma būtība:* noteikumos norādīt, ka vadītājs veic _pārvadāšanas pakalpojumu_, nevis pasta pakalpojumu.
* *Platformas statuss:* Bolt darbojas kā _digitāla starpniecības platforma_, kas savieno lietotājus, nevis kā pasta komersants.
* *Procesa struktūra:* nav pasta pavaddokumenta, saņemšanas paraksta vai centralizētas šķirošanas.

----

h3. *3. Attiecīgais tiesiskais regulējums*

Šāda pieeja balstās uz:

* *Pasta likuma 1. panta* izņēmuma robežām (neattiecas uz neadresētiem vai nelieliem priekšmetiem);
* *Autopārvadājumu likuma* normām par *vieglā transportlīdzekļa pārvadājumiem* (neattiecas uz pasažieru taksometru papildu darbībām nelielā apjomā);
* *MK noteikumiem Nr. 599*, kas nosaka, ka taksometru pārvadājumi ar vieglo automobili var ietvert papildu pakalpojumus, ja tie neizmaina pakalpojuma būtību.

----

h3. *4. Praktiskā drošības formula*

Pakalpojumu aprakstā un noteikumos ieteicams skaidri norādīt:

{quote}“*Bolt Send* ir transporta pakalpojums, kas nodrošina nelielu priekšmetu pārvadāšanu starp divām adresēm, izmantojot vieglos transportlīdzekļus.
Pakalpojums nav klasificējams kā pasta vai kravu pārvadājums saskaņā ar *Pasta likumu* vai *Autopārvadājumu likumu*.”{quote}

Šādā modelī:

* Vadītāji *nav jāpārreģistrē kā pasta komersanti vai kravu pārvadātāji*;
* *SPRK* uzraudzība uz šo pakalpojumu *neattiecas*, jo tas neietver adresētu sūtījumu piegādi;
* *VID un Autotransporta direkcijas* licences nav nepieciešamas, jo tas neiekļaujas komerckravu pārvadājumu kategorijā.

----

h3. *5. Riska robeža*

Ja praksē “Bolt Send” tiktu lietots kā *pilnvērtīgs kurjerpasts* (adresēta sūtījuma nogāde ar saņemšanas apstiprinājumu), *SPRK* var interpretēt to kā pasta pakalpojumu pēc būtības.
Tāpēc drošāk:

* Saglabāt *vienkāršu transporta pakalpojuma modeli* (A → B bez adresāta apstiprinājuma);
* Izvairīties no *pasta terminoloģijas un procedūrām*;
* Nodrošināt, ka *vadītāji paliek taksometra licence ietvaros* un *nav jāreģistrējas papildu režīmos*.

----

h3. ✅ *Secinājums*

{quote}Ja “Bolt Send” tiek noformēts kā *mazgabarīta priekšmetu pārvadājums ar vieglo automobili*,
neizmantojot *pasta vai kravu pārvadājumu elementus*,
tad:

* *Nav nepieciešama SPRK reģistrācija kā pasta komersantam;*
* *Nav jāsaņem komerckravu licence;*
* *Vadītāji var darboties esošā taksometra reģistrācijas ietvaros.*{quote}

Overview of main changes:

# *30-Day Termination Notice Added in Multiple Clauses*

* Added a requirement for the Lessor to provide the Lessee with a thirty (30) day prior written termination notice in two key situations:
** *Art. 20(1)* – when regulatory or legal changes make it impossible to use the advertising space.
** *Art. 24(2)* – when the Lessor loses rights over the advertising space (e.g., their contract with the owner ends).
This strengthens Bolt’s position by ensuring it receives advance notice before termination takes effect.

# *Competitor Advertising Clause Improved (Art. 20(2))*

* Replaced the previous full waiver of liability with a new obligation on the Lessor to prevent competitor placements on or near Bolt’s advertising surfaces.
* Added remedies for Bolt if this obligation is breached — the right to:
** request replacement of the affected advertising space at no additional cost, or
** terminate the campaign and receive a proportional refund.

# *Extended Payment-Delay Period and Balanced Termination Rights (Art. 22(2))*

* Increased the grace period before termination for non-payment from 20 days to 30 days.
* Added the requirement for the Lessor to give a 30-day prior written notice before unilateral termination due to payment delay, ensuring Bolt has time to remedy defaults.

# *Adjusted Approval Period for Printed Materials (Art. 15(2))*

* The response time for Bolt’s approval of advertising materials was extended from 1 day to 15 days, preventing automatic approval by default if the team cannot review promptly.

# *Confidentiality Clause Refined (Art. 28)*

* The fixed monetary penalty was removed.
* Replaced with a case-by-case indemnification standard (“full indemnity for actual damages and lost profits”), making liability proportionate to the breach.

hi [~accountid:712020:d008dcec-6cfe-47e4-83a0-c29522744742] , thanks a lot for this! I’m aligned with your assessment and I do not think that this change much fromTax Fin.Reg. perspective. Please just below some points it would be good to add in your assessment.

h4. *1. Reclassification Risk*

The model add some reclassification risk due to the *performance-linked variable component* of the compensation. However, the presence of a *€100 fixed monthly fee*, payable regardless of the number of rides completed, *mitigates the concern previously raised* by outside counsel regarding unpaid "free advertising." That risk arose when drivers received *no compensation at all* unless they completed rides — a setup which courts could interpret as a sign of dependency on the platform. Maintaining a fixed fee component helps support the framing of the relationship as a commercial agreement for advertising services, rather than employment.

Nonetheless, the *performance-based variable fee* must continue to be positioned carefully to avoid legal ambiguity. Courts may still scrutinize any compensation model that appears to incentivize exclusive or majority engagement with the platform.

h4. *2. VAT and Tax Compliance*

Advertising services in France are taxed at the *standard 20% VAT rate*, compared to the *10% rate applicable to transport services*. Shifting from a commission refund to a per-ride bonus structure *risks obscuring the nature of the compensation*, unless it is clearly defined in all agreements and communications as remuneration for *advertising services.*

*Recommended Actions:*

* Frame both the fixed and variable payments as *advertising income*.
* Ensure contractual documents and driver-facing communications *consistently reflect this positioning*.

h3. *Implementation of the Tiered Offer*

h4. a) *Contractual Acceptance*

Allowing acceptance by performance (e.g. sending photo verification of sticker placement) is practical, but presents enforceability risks—particularly *within the first month*, before a clear pattern of acceptance is established.

*Mitigation Measures:*

* Distribute the updated insertion order and general conditions *before program rollout*.
* Implement a workflow to *log timestamped proof of contract delivery* (via email or in-app notification), to document consent in case of dispute.

h4. b) *Operational Controls and Reclassification*

Tying variable payments to the presence of stickers—verified through monthly photo checks—may raise concerns of *control and oversight*, two core elements courts consider when evaluating a potential employment relationship. While this alone does not create a subordination link, it contributes to a broader “faisceau d’indices” (body of evidence).

*Mitigation Measures:*

* Maintain sticker verification as a *condition for payment*, but *do not apply penalties* for non-compliance. Simply *withhold the advertising payment* for that period.
* Avoid any contractual language that suggests sanctioning or obligating drivers to affix stickers.
* Allow drivers to *exit the program unilaterally at any time*, without a minimum term, to support the independent contractor framework.

Hope this makes sense. Happy to further discuss.

`thanks,

Eli

Thanks [~accountid:712020:186ae0de-e4be-463c-8680-879b2f40f45f] , my thoughts on the subjects would be

# *Snackbar actions should be reachable after the currently focused element, but they should not forcibly steal focus.* 
## On web, if the user is interacting with another control (typing in a form) and the Snackbar appears, its action buttons should enter the natural tab order only if the user presses {{TAB}} again.
## On mobile, screen reader users should be able to swipe to reach Snackbar content and buttons, but focus shouldn’t jump automatically.
# I know that swipe-to-dismiss is common on Android, but isn’t as common on iOS. *Consistency wise I would prefer an actual dismiss button "X" or "Dismiss"/"Close" button*.
# Love the idea of dismiss duration calculations! I’m thinking something along the lines of these:
## Short (less than 100 char.) and/or no action buttons – 5s
## Long (more than 100 char.) and/or buttons – 8-12s
## Critical (user must act or distructive) – manual dismissal only
# Countdown timer - I personally feel like it’s a bit overkill as it creates more visual noise, but we can discuss this further
# *I would say let’s show only one at a time, but we can queue them*. Stacking multiple Snackbars simultaneously creates accessibility problems, particularly for screen reader users and violates success criteria around timing, focus order and live region management. 
## *Screen reader overload* - “If multiple toast messages are announced simultaneously or close together, screen readers may interrupt the first with the second, resulting in a loss of information.” [https://adrianroselli.com/2020/01/defining-toast-messages.html|https://adrianroselli.com/2020/01/defining-toast-messages.html|smart-link] 
## *WCAG 2.2 Timing SC 2.2.1* - If multiple Snackbars appear, especially with auto-dismiss timers, users cannot adjust or respond before the Snackbar disappears. [https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/timing-adjustable.html|https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/timing-adjustable.html|smart-link] 
## *Focus order* - If 2-3 Snackbars show at once, each with buttons it introduces: unpredictable tab order, repeated interruptions and difficulty understanding what button belongs to what message. This breaks operability, especially for keyboard-only and screen reader users. [https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-order.html|https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-order.html|smart-link] 
## *Live region conflicts* - only one {{aria-live="assertive"}} or {{role="alert"}} region should be active at a time. Stacked Snackbars=multiple simultaneous live regions → screen reader confusion.

Hi again [~accountid:5da0457ec62f840db2b704a9], I’ve discussed this matter with Central Legal and: 

We currently maintain a general *age restriction (18+) across all EU markets*, as the principles for entering into contracts with minors are largely harmonised within the EU. It is legally complex to conclude binding contracts with individuals under 18, and we also do not have mechanisms in place to verify or record parental consent.

From a *regulatory and compliance* perspective, the age restriction in the T&Cs serves several important purposes beyond national transport laws:

* *Privacy:* The age restriction supports our privacy compliance position, as it allows us to assert that we do not process personal data of minors, which would otherwise require additional safeguards and parental consent mechanisms.
* *DSA (Digital Services Act):* It helps us avoid triggering additional obligations related to minors under the DSA, such as the need to apply enhanced protection or design-specific measures.

For these reasons, we *strongly recommend keeping the age restriction in the T&Cs unchanged*, +even+ if underage riders are legally permitted to use taxis in Finland.

That said, this does not necessarily require us to actively suspend or terminate all underage riders. Until we develop a compliant and technically feasible way to manage parental consent and related processes, we can maintain the restriction in the T&Cs without enforcing it strictly.

Please note that this matter is already on Central Legal’s longer-term roadmap, as achieving full compliance will require cross-team collaboration and significant tech development.

Let me know if you have questions!

Summary of the initiative as explained by you last week (please correct me if the below is incorrect):

* Branding commission would be set out in a tiered offer structured as detailed in Matteo’s message above;
* You would first roll this out for testing purposes with one or two fleets that include both existing drivers with branded cars, and drivers that are not part of the branding program.


--> +*Legal assessment of the tiered offer*+*:*

* The *fixed monthly fee* ensures that the remuneration is *not purely performance-based*, which helps *mitigate reclassification risks* under French labour law.
* Regarding the *variable fee*, the underlying structure remains that of a *payment for an advertising service*, not a refund or commission rebate. The only change is the *metric used* (rides completed instead of a percentage of Bolt service fees). The service therefore continues to qualify as an *advertising space rental*, subject to the *standard VAT rate (20%)*, rather than as a transport or payment service.



--> +*Implementation of the tiered offer*+:

To roll out the tiered offer, we recommend a structured contractual update aligned with legal requirements and operational practicality:

* *New drivers:* a *new Special Terms Agreement* will be prepared to reflect the updated tiered payment model. All new drivers joining the two pilot fleets must *accept these Special Terms* upon onboarding (via the existing Typeform flow or a similar digital acceptance mechanism). {color:#bf2600}→ Are you able to do this only for some drivers that are part of the fleet you will test this with?{color}
* *Existing drivers:* current drivers already under the Branded Car program will be *notified by email* of the new conditions, with the updated Special Terms attached. Drivers will be informed that *continuing to send the monthly photo to claim payment* constitutes *acceptance by performance*, replicating the valid process implemented earlier this year.

❗ As this is a test, we ask that you keep it to one or two fleets, and based on the testing results, we can assess together how this should be rolled out to a larger group or all of the drivers on the programme. 


As a  reminder of the implications of this program, please review the general feedback below: 

h4. *1.* +*Reclassification Risk*+

The model adds some reclassification risk due to the *performance-linked variable component* of the compensation. However, the presence of a *€100 fixed monthly fee*, payable regardless of the number of rides completed, *mitigates the concern previously raised* by outside counsel regarding unpaid "free advertising." That risk arose when drivers received *no compensation at all* unless they completed rides — a setup which courts could interpret as a sign of dependency on the platform. Maintaining a fixed fee component helps support the framing of the relationship as a commercial agreement for advertising services, rather than employment.

Nonetheless, the *performance-based variable fee* must continue to be positioned carefully to avoid legal ambiguity. Courts may still scrutinize any compensation model that appears to incentivize exclusive or majority engagement with the platform.

h4. *2.* +*VAT and Tax Compliance*+

Advertising services in France are taxed at the *standard 20% VAT rate*, compared to the *10% rate applicable to transport services*. Shifting from a commission refund to a per-ride bonus structure *risks obscuring the nature of the compensation*, unless it is clearly defined in all agreements and communications as remuneration for *advertising services.*

*Recommended Actions:*

* Frame both the fixed and variable payments as *advertising income*.
* Ensure contractual documents and driver-facing communications *consistently reflect this positioning*.

*3.* +*Implementation of the Tiered Offer*+

h4. a) *Contractual Acceptance*

Allowing acceptance by performance (e.g. sending photo verification of sticker placement) is practical, but presents enforceability risks—particularly *within the first month*, before a clear pattern of acceptance is established.

*Mitigation Measures:*

* Distribute the updated insertion order and general conditions *before program rollout*.
* Implement a workflow to *log timestamped proof of contract delivery* (via email or in-app notification), to document consent in case of dispute.

h4. b) *Operational Controls and Reclassification*

Tying variable payments to the presence of stickers—verified through monthly photo checks—may raise concerns of *control and oversight*, two core elements courts consider when evaluating a potential employment relationship. While this alone does not create a subordination link, it contributes to a broader “faisceau d’indices” (body of evidence).

*Mitigation Measures:*

* Maintain sticker verification as a *condition for payment*, but *do not apply penalties* for non-compliance. 
* Avoid any contractual language that suggests sanctioning or obligating drivers to affix stickers.
* Allow drivers to *exit the program unilaterally at any time*, without a minimum term, to support the independent contractor framework.


If you have any questions on the above, please let us know, happy to discuss further.

# *Lawful basis for disclosure* 

The request invokes Schedule 2 Part 1 Section 2 of the Data Protection Act 2018, which allows processing where “necessary for the prevention or detection of crime” or “the apprehension or prosecution of offenders.”
This provides a law-enforcement exemption under Article 23 GDPR (UK) and Schedule 2 DPA 2018, not a standalone legal obligation.
Therefore, disclosure must rely on our legitimate interests, namely the legitimate interest of MCC in investigating a criminal offence, balanced against the driver’s rights. In other words, the legal basis is not valid, but we have options to share data - see below.

*2. What I advise to share if we decided to share data*

* Vehicle activity confirmation and driver identification (name + licence number) are proportionate and necessary to verify who was operating the vehicle.
* Booking records for the specific 2.5 hour window are narrowly scoped and proportionate.
* Contact details:
** Recommend providing the email address rather than the phone number or home address unless MCC demonstrates a clear necessity (e.g., serving a statutory notice).
** Phone numbers and residential addresses pose higher privacy risks and are rarely essential for such enquiries.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. Final Recommendation
{panel}

*Disclosure may proceed* *only* if limited to:

* Confirmation of vehicle activity (active / inactive)
* Driver name and PHV licence number
* Relevant booking records (03:00–05:30 only)
* *Email address only* for contact purposes

*Do not disclose* phone number or home address unless MCC later justifies necessity under a specific statutory power.

# Campaign type: “Fleet campaigns vs fleet courier campaigns” 
## Fleet-level campaigns look like B2B arrangements: Bolt incentivises another business (the fleet) to meet service-level expectations. The fleet then decides _how_ to achieve that, including how to motivate its couriers and how to divide the bonuses. That keeps Bolt’s role at arm’s length and supports the “no employment relationship” narrative. Low-medium risk 
## Fleet courier campaigns: Even if the fleet is technically the messenger, if Bolt defines the courier’s performance targets and funds the incentive, it looks like Bolt is managing individual workers through rewards. High risk 
#  Coordination Requirements: unless there’s a specific format agreed in the fleet agreement, then whatever form works. Written form is preferred, in case of any miscommunication or disputes. 
# Does the campaign copy require Legal approval before launch? If possible, legal should review the template draft (but not each individual message). 
# Can we select (cherry-pick) specific couriers or must targeting be at the city or fleet level? 
## Not cherry-picking is the least risky approach. 
## If you do wish to cherry-pick, then the picking should be done at least at a fleet level.  If we start hand-selecting _specific couriers_ within a fleet — for example, “top-performing couriers in Fleet X and Y” — that starts to look like Bolt is directly managing people, not contracting with a business. 
# Campaign type
## X get Y type of campaigns carry less risk. 
## AR-based campaigns are high risk.
# Communication - from a reclass perspective, it will probably not make a big difference whether the we are sending continuous pushes or the standard comms. The risky part is that we are sending comms directly to couriers in the first place. 

The safest setup - from a reclassification standpoint - is *fleet-level, output-based (“do X, get Y”) campaigns*, with clear B2B framing and communication going through fleets and the fleets receiving these incentives.  If you wish to take the higher risk approach, then please note that this means accepting a higher reclassification risk, which can be used against us in future proceedings.

Hey [~accountid:712020:9cfda827-f644-48a1-9da8-aff3fd427bf9] !
Thanks for raising this — After aligning with Central Legal, here’s our legal view on the proposed campaign structures in Portugal:

*Campaign Type: Fleet vs Fleet-Courier Campaigns*
+Fleet-Level Campaigns+
These resemble a B2B arrangement: Bolt incentivizes a fleet (as a business partner) to meet agreed service levels. The fleet then independently decides how to manage its couriers and allocate the incentive.
This structure maintains clear legal separation between Bolt and individual couriers and supports our position that there is no employment relationship.
*→ Legal Risk: Low to Medium*

+Fleet-Courier Campaigns (Bonuses Paid to Couriers, Communicated via Fleet)+
Even if the fleet communicates the campaign, if Bolt sets courier-level performance targets and pays the bonus directly to couriers, this creates the appearance that Bolt is managing individual workers through rewards.
That is a key risk factor for employment reclassification.
*→ Legal Risk: High*

*Coordination Requirements*
Unless a specific communication format is required in the fleet agreement, any method is acceptable — but written confirmation is strongly preferred, to ensure clarity and traceability.

*Campaign Copy Approval*
If possible, legal should review the template draft (but not each individual message).

*Targeting rules:*
To minimize risk, avoid cherry-picking individual couriers;
If targeting is necessary, then the picking should be done at the fleet or regional level, not by courier name.
If Bolt selects individual couriers (e.g., “top-performers in Fleet X”), it further reinforces the perception of direct management which increases the risks.

*Campaign type:*
- “*Do X, Get Y*” volume-based campaigns are *less risky* and preferred.
- Campaigns based on *acceptance rate or other SLAs* are *higher risk*, as they resemble performance management.

*Communication*
The legal risk doesn’t come from how frequently we communicate, but from the fact that Bolt is addressing couriers directly about performance incentives.
Where possible, communications should be routed through the fleet, with Bolt avoiding direct courier outreach — particularly via the app.

*In conclusion:* 
The *safest approach* — from a reclassification perspective — is to run fleet-level, output-based campaigns, with:
- Incentives paid to fleets,
- No courier-level performance targets set by Bolt, and
- Communication handled by the fleet.

However, if the business decides to proceed with courier-level targeting and direct payments, then please note that this means accepting a higher reclassification risk, which can be used against us in future proceedings.

{quote}Dear *Martin,* 



Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *4 October 2025*, in which you asked for information about the following:



# Why are photos taken during the identity verification process stored by Bolt instead of keeping only verification result (success / fail)
# Why are photos of expired documents from previous verifications stored
# Why Bolt Food delivery invoices contain full names of Couriers and their email addresses



*Response to Question 1 & 2*



Bolt keeps the photos taken during the verification process and photos from previous verifications for the following reasons:



# *Legal and Compliance Requirements*



Operating carsharing services requires Bolt to demonstrate that user identity was properly verified and that they held a valid driver’s license at the time of the verification and car rental. Storing verification photos enables us to: 



* Comply with applicable laws and regulatory requirements;
* Respond to requests from law enforcement or supervisory authorities;
* Demonstrate compliance and defend ourselves against potential legal claims or disputes. 



# *Fraud prevention, security, historical record and audit trail*



Storing the verification photos allows Bolt to investigate and resolve potential fraud or identity misuse and detect repeated or coordinated attempts to submit falsified or altered documents. Additionally, maintaining verification photos allows us to conduct audits to ensure our verification systems function correctly and maintain a historical record that supports investigations into suspicious activity or account misuse. 



# *Quality assurance and system improvement*



Past data helps us review and strengthen our verification systems, making them more effective against evolving fraud attempts.



For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/|smart-link] , which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.



*Response to Question 3*



Full name information is mandated by the applicable laws. In Estonia, if a Courier is a VAT taxable person, they must comply with the Value Added Tax Act that sets out what information must be included in the invoice. Bolt acts as an agent of the Couriers in the administration of the Bolt Food Platform in relation to the mediation of Delivery Contracts between the Couriers and the Customers, including preparation of invoices for delivery services to the Client.



Thank you for bringing the fact that Courier emails are included in the User personal data export. We appreciate you taking time to flag this detail. We are already working on updating the personal data export to ensure Courier emails are no longer included in the invoices.



*Deletion request*



In your data subject rights request from *4 October 2025* you also requested a deletion of your personal data. In response to your deletion request, we want to inform you that your account will be scheduled for deletion and will be deleted within 30 days. All personal data linked to your profile has been erased. However, please be aware that certain personal data may be retained in accordance with the relevant data protection regulations, even after the account deletion. For details about the retention periods of your personal data, please refer to our Privacy Notice at [https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/|smart-link] .



*Your rights* 



If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.





Yours sincerely,



Bolt{quote}

*Data gathered - Looker*:
- KM ridden + Orders per each model, per each city - source [Explore Orders|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/explore/rental/order_order]
- from Looker we get information on the AVG vehicles on street daily - source [Explore Micromobility KPIs|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/explore/rental/etl_micromobility_business_kpi_daily]
both this data sets are grouped in monthly periods.

_With these data sets we calculate_:
- city metrics
    1. RpV
    2. KM per Ride
    3. AVG vehicles with rides
- seasonality
    1. Specific month impact vs the average for the metrices above

The idea is that with the forecasted data provided by Regional Managers (fleet size and rides expected in a specific city in 2026) we can apply the seasonal trends and forecast the Nr of Rides and AVG vehicles on street.

_We calculated data and seasonality at three levels_:
- city level
- country level
- network level

_How do we use the city levels_:
- If a city has collected data for more than 50k rides and 6 months in the past 12 months for a vehicle type, we consider this data trustworthy;
- If not (might be due to a new city launch or a fleet swap in the city), we check the country situation. When the country has at least 2 cities with more than 50k rides and 6 month usage of a vehicly type, we consider the country data trustworthy and apply the same to the new city.
- If not (might be a new country launch such as London Ebikes or Kazakhstan’s Valks) we take network data
This calculation gives us the ability to mitigate the lack of data at a city level, relying on what we currently gathered at country or network levels.
The more a fleet will be ridden in a city, the more specific data we gather and we will be able to be more specific with sending parts to the specific city.

[{color:#bf2600}_WIP IMPROVEMENT_{color}] - for forecasting metrices based on the fleet size, use forecasted fleet size rather than the Vehicles on street.

_We calculated data at two levels_:
- city level
- network level

This calculation gives us the ability to mitigate the lack of data at a city level, relying on what we currently gathered at network level.
The more a fleet will be ridden in a city, the more specific data we gather and we will be able to be more specific with sending parts to the specific city.

The idea is to keep km based and actual consumption calculations close to each other in the dashboard, to track both trends.

h2. General

The *short term effect* on driver behavior (and marketplace) of *showing less price details on acceptance screen is positive*. The long term effects however are less known to us and much more difficult to quantify. Current situation in Azerbaijan is that Bolt market share is ~67%. Bolt’s acceptance screen is very transparent showing both gross and net prices, drop off location, payment method, rider name and rating while Uber allegedly shows none of that. Whether acceptance screen visibility has anything to do with our high market share is up for debate but as a driver I would for sure prefer the company that shows me the price over the one that doesn’t.

Short term known effects (not statistically significant here but almost every AB test from every market shows similar results):

* Net price vs no price - better to not show price at all
* Net price vs both net + gross price - better to only show net price

Azerbaijan went (I assume) from gross to net + gross on March 11, 2025 → [Slack thread|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C07CHLDLWJG/p1741606398554859]

Proposal to move to net only on July 23rd, 2025 was put on hold on July 21st → [Slack thread|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C07CHLDLWJG/p1753102649218889] and screenshot:

Generally if we go from not showing price to showing price the short term effects are negative (driver cancellation+rejection rate goes up, avg finished orders goes down). *However*… the AB test scorecard _doesn’t show any significant results_ so maybe the Confluence page is wrong. Either way, huge grain of salt.

h2. Conclusion

Running more tests on price visibility in Azerbaijan and Baku doesn’t necessarily seem like a must do thing, there have already been tests regarding this. Unless something has fundamentally changed (which I assume there’s not a lot of things affecting price visibility effects) then there’s very little to be found out via testing.

-Interestingly the mapping shows that dynamic commission is live at the same time. The assumption so far has been that for dynamic commission we would have to be on net price only. So I’d be very curious how this is working out.- ➡️ Update: it’s not live there

Generally

* Removing both net and gross price from acceptance screen completely would yield positive short term results most likely. However the long term effects could be less than great as there is potential to starting to lose supply.
* Removing both net and gross price from acceptance screen for lowest tier or for the first X rides could be up for discussion.
* Removing gross price from the acceptance screen would probably be a good direction to push towards. Short term it might affect drivers negatively as they see smaller numbers only and the human brain isn’t always great at thinking fully logically. However to be able to have more aggressive dynamic commission limits it would be pretty much necessary as for high commission rides would most likely perform very poorly conversion wise.
* In case we do have supply problems/drivers preferring competition could we build comms around our better visibility being the perk why they should prefer us?

*Next steps:*

# Please review the correspondence with the Partner to see if we discussed the purpose of the sign-up bonus in writing. If we did, please share with me the correspondence (screenshots or forward the email chain).
# Once 1 is done, I will prepare the termination notice based on termination right provided in clause 3.3.3 where the basis of termination would be a material breach of the Agreement. We will either say that clause 1.2 of the Agreement was breached or clause 1.2 and prior correspondence regarding the purpose of the sign-up bonus constitute the material breach. The Partner will have one month to remedy the breach (which will reduce the amount of the sign-up bonus that we can claim back). If the they signed exclusivity agreement they will not be able to remedy the breach, i.e. resume operations on Bolt Food platform.

Depending on the Partner's reaction to our notice the following consequences will apply:

* If the Partner will resume operations on the platform we will not be entitled to the sign-up bonus and the agreement will continue to be in force.
* If the Partner will dispute the reason for termination (which they can) we can only go to court to argue that the reason for termination is correct and we are entitled to receive part of the sign-up bonus back.
* If the Partner will not dispute the reason for termination, but will not return the sign-up bonus we would need to go to court to claim the sign-up bonus. In theory, we may consider debt collection agency too.
* The best case scenario is that the Partner will return the reduced amount of the sign-up bonus, we will not be able to recover the full amount. 

{quote}*Legal analysis*
The agreement does not incorporate General Terms and Special Terms as the reference to these is vague and the terms used are not defined. Therefore, the "Agreement" is a standalone agreement that incorporates all the terms. 

The sign-up bonus can be claimed back only in case of termination of the Agreement as per clause 3.4. Since General Terms do not apply to this Agreement and provision B in the Background section specifies that the terms of the Agreement shall prevail the Agreement can be terminated only in accordance with section 3 of the Agreement. 

Clause 3.2 specifies that parties are not allowed to terminate the agreement without a cause. Clause 3.3 sets out the conditions under which the agreement can be terminated:

Clause 3.3.1 allows Bolt to terminate the Agreement if Partner fails to meet SLAs for two consecutive months or for any two months within 6 months period. In this Agreement, the SLAs are 98% Acceptance Rate and 95% Availability Rate. Both terms are not defined and are vague, therefore, can be interpreted in a variety of ways. The Agreement was concluded on 24th of September 2025 and Partner is inactive on the Bolt Food platform since 3rd of October, therefore, Bolt cannot use this cause for termination as less than two months has passed since non-compliance. 

Clause 3.3.2 allows Bolt to terminate the Agreement in case the Partner enters into any exclusivity agreement with a third party delivery platform. Unless Partner explicitly confirms having an exclusive agreement Bolt has no way of checking whether the Partner has entered into an exclusivity agreement without court interference. The Partner can say that they simply don't want to work with Bolt and other platforms.

Clause 3.3.3 allows Bolt to terminate the Agreement in case the Partner materially breaches any provision of the Agreement and fails to remedy such breach within 30 days of written notice from Bolt. There are several clauses that could potentially be used to allege a material breach of the Agreement:
Clause 1.1 requires Partner to invest 20% of its GMV generated via Bolt Food platform into delivery discount campaigns. Unspent amounts shall roll over to the next month and compliance shall be evaluated in "four 6-month" periods. Partner has not breached this provision as obligation to invest GMV does not arise if they do not operate on the platform. Also, even if some GMV was generated while Partner was active on the platform the obligation to invest will simply roll over to the next month and at the time of compliance review it cannot be alleged that Partner did anything wrong as the obligation to invest is too vague.
Clause 1.2 requires Partner to meet SLAs. SLAs are 98% Acceptance Rate and 95% Availability Rate. Both terms are not defined and are vague, therefore, can be interpreted in a variety of ways. Even if there is a slight chance of arguing that by Availability Rate we mean Partner's availability on the platform we have failed to provide the method of calculating the rate. The Partner can argue that the rate is calculated as a % of time that Partner was available within the first week from signing the Agreement. We can only argue that the interpretation and method of calculation shall derive from parties intentions made in good faith.
Clause 1.3 requires Partner not to enter into exclusivity agreements with third-party online food delivery platform that would restrict Partner's ability to operate on Bolt's or any other platform. Unless we have a proof of existence of such agreement we cannot allege that there was a breach of this clause.

Considering the above clause 1.2 is the clause that we can try arguing and terminate the agreement as per clause 3.3.3. Otherwise, if there is evidence in a form of written correspondence clearly stating the reason why the sign-up bonus was paid that is to ensure that the Partner shall exclusively operate on the Bolt Food platform we can argue that the Partner's actions are not in line with the essence of the Agreement and also terminate the Agreement based on clause 3.3.3. However, in both cases, the Partner has 30 days to remedy the breach, i.e. resume it's operations on the platform in which case the Partner will not be obliged to return the payment Bolt made to the Partner. In addition to that, any delay of termination will reduce the amount that the Partner is obliged to repay. There is nothing that would stop the Partner from ceasing operations again after resuming them as described and reducing the amount that should be returned even further.{quote}
