[^2025.11 Bolt Operations Evertogether NDA (reviewed by Bolt).docx]

+*PRELIMINARY ANALYSIS (03.11)*+

* General:
** *Transparency*: Not in privacy notice. As such, disclaimer language would be helpful.
** *Auto-enrolment* (non-SCD): Fine if mandatory.
*** On the understanding that Bolt, as an “employer”, is required to implement auto-enrolled pension scheme, then we can rely on compliance with a legal obligation here (but I would like to understand a bit more about the law).
*** If this is a legal obligation, I struggle to see how ADM rules would be triggered. In any case, if this is the UK, our only concern here would be SCD anyway due to recent legislative changes (although a DPIA may be helpful).
** *SCD*: We may be sharing driver SCD with Zellis, as well as possibly A10 data.
*** If mandatory, then we may be able to rely on necessity in the context of employment or social security law / occupational pension schemes (rather than consent).
*** However, we would still need an “appropriate policy document” which (i) explains how we ensure that A5 data processing principles are adhered to; and (ii) indicating retention periods / erasure.
* Zellis Agreement (new - [link|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fPFoko6Ea8KdV38O45-n0wPRjxrXurkdkTSjEcozWw8/edit?tab=t.0])
** Main Agreement:
*** Liability:
**** Clause 10.2: Each party’s total aggregate liability shall not exceed 12 months' fees. This is too low ⚠️ 
***** NB. Legal has already suggested changing this to 2x fees or £2m, whichever is higher. This is fine from my POV 💡 
**** Clause 10.3: No liability for indirect losses. Not a huge deal, but something worth pushing back on in the first instance ⚠️ 
**** No data privacy / data breach indemnities. This is a big issue, given the volume of data being shared ⚠️ 
***** NB. Legal has already suggested including such an indemnity 💡 
** Data Protection Schedule:
*** Zellis is listed as the processor (on behalf of Bolt) for all purposes except for collecting Bolt contact details in administering the agreement - this makes sense 💡 
*** Complies with provisions of Article 28 GDPR, except there are no explicit audit provisions ⚠️ 
*** Clause 5.3: Where Bolt accesses Zellis' services from outside of the UK/EEA, it is Bolt’s responsibility to ensure that international data transfer requirements are met - this is only a problem if we are accessing from a third country (which we are likely not, but worth checking) ⚠️ 
*** Clause 7.1: DSRR assistance is at Bolt’s expense - we cannot accept this, as it is a GDPR requirement ⚠️ 
*** Clause 7.2: Zellis must inform Bolt of DSRRs “promptly” - it would be better to have a specific deadline ⚠️ 
*** Clause 8.1: Zellis must inform Bolt of PDBs “without undue delay” - again, we should set a deadline ⚠️ 
*** Clause 9.1: Zellis assistance to A32-36 obligations is at Bolt’s expense - we cannot accept this, as it is a GDPR requirement ⚠️ 
*** Clause 10.2: Bolt approves “Approved Subprocessors” ([here|http://solutions.zellis.com/subprocessorlist]). Mostly UK/EEA, but some in India / Philippines / USA / New Zealand. I would prefer to only approve UK/EEA ones for now, but we might concede on this ⚠️ 
*** Clause 10.3: Bolt can object to new sub-processors within 10 days (not specific authorisation). If Bolt objects, costs of finding a new one are on Bolt. Also, unclear how Bolt is notified of new sub-processors ⚠️ 
*** Unclear whether InfoSec has approved the security schedule ([here|http://solutions.zellis.com/securityschedule]) ⚠️ 
*** Appendix 1 sets out the data processing specifics. May include passport number, citizenship, and entitlement to work data (could be criminal records?). In any case, SCD explicitly listed as possible data categories - as such, need to dig into whether we are actually transferring these. 
* Aviva Agreement (needs to be changed):
** I have not yet seen this. Need to clarify what needs to be changed.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*NEXT STEPS*
{panel}

* Questions ([here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09KXK4DV60/p1762188941452099]):
** What law(s) say that Bolt should be considered an employer, and should implement an auto-enrolment pension scheme? Is this now an explicit legal obligation (to auto enrol), or is it optional under the law? Can drivers opt out?
** Which countries (Bolt, Zellis and drivers) are in scope here - is it just the UK?
** What specific categories of personal data are we sharing here? Are we actually sharing any SCD?
** Where is the Aviva agreement? What needs to be done there?
* Advice:
** Key risks generally are as follows:
*** Auto-enrolment: Should be ok, provided that it is mandatory.
*** SCD: If mandatory, we should be covered on legal basis, but we would still need an *appropriate policy document* (also possible a DPIA).
*** Transparency: Not mentioned in the privacy notice, so we should consider *disclaimer language* when notifying drivers. Long term, we can update the privacy notice (see rough draft below - discuss with wider team first - consider whether we already have pensions and if so how this is covered).
** Zellis Agreement needs to be amended:
*** *Security*: InfoSec should review the security schedule to confirm that they are happy.
*** *Subprocessors*: We should ensure more of a shift to specific, rather than general, authorisation.
*** *Audits*: The agreement needs to contain an obligation on Zellis to allow for and contribute to audits (this is legally mandatory).
*** *Costs*: The agreement currently states that DSSR/A32-36 assistance is at Bolt’s expense. We cannot accept this, as they are legally mandatory.
*** *Notification Deadlines*: The agreement does not contain specific deadlines for Zellis to inform Bolt about DSRRs/PDBs.
*** *Indemnities / Liability*: As advised by Legal already, we need a pro-Bolt privacy indemnity and a higher liability cap for Zellis.

Works as expected:

* Instance created without specifying the termination protection gets created with {{disable_api_termination=false}}
* Setting {{disable_termination=true}} in the instance module arguments changes resource parameter {{disable_api_termination}} to {{true}} (enables termination protection)
* Destroying instance with enabled termination protection fails
* Destroying instance with disabled termination protection (default) works

Error when destroying the instance with termination protection:

{quote}Error: terminating EC2 Instance (i-097cabb53bfc28322):

  operation error EC2: TerminateInstances,

  https response error StatusCode: 400,

  RequestID: 11c0ec8e-2b40-426b-9248-e3b00b254841,

  api error OperationNotPermitted:

    The instance 'i-097cabb53bfc28322' may not be terminated.

    Modify its 'disableApiTermination' instance attribute and try again.{quote}

----

{{force_destroy}} (defaults to false) is needed to return the old behavior – Terraform can destroy the instance with enabled termination protection if {{force_destroy=true}} is set.

Docs: [https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/aws/latest/docs/resources/instance#force_destroy-1|https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/aws/latest/docs/resources/instance#force_destroy-1|smart-link].

It is not exposed by our {{instance}} module and therefore cannot be set in the projects; instead, {{disable_termination=true}} should be removed before deleting int instance (same as before).

Hey [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a] - thanks for your input😌 here are a few of my ideas:

{quote}* _I highly doubt there is a way that we could word the comms to frame them as service / administrative messages (i.e., non-marketing).Ultimately, the things we are pushing here are part of a third-party loyalty rewards program, and so a purposive approach would always lead to the conclusion that the comms are promotional. This is particularly likely in Poland, Romania and France, which are all high risk countries regarding marketing comms._
* _Not naming the specific offer providers does not change anything here. We would still be promoting Bolt Rewards, and so the comms would still count as marketing._
* {color:#4c9aff}*_Conclusion_*{color}_: IMO this is always going to be interpreted as marketing. If we want to get around the consent issue, our focus should be on promoting Bot Rewards through less direct means (i.e., more creative uses of general advertising, in-time requests for consent to marketing comms, etc.)._{quote}

I think main question here is not whether this can be avoided the label of “marketing” but rather “third party” marketing. In my view, the safest thing to do here would be to simply promote the functionality of “Partner Offers” inside Bolt app - a place where Bolt drivers can check offers special bonuses & discounts exclusively provided to drivers who drive with Bolt. I think it can be carefully worded to minimise risks of promoting third parties but giving drivers a bit more detail to entice them.

A more risk (but still possible option) in my view would be to take the approach identical to Bolt Delivery, where we made the decision to promote exclusive offers of merchants/products that are being sold in Bolt Delivery app - i.e. Coca-Cola discounts, Auchan discounts (i.e. no fee delivery).

Reasoning could be that, again, “Partner Offers” is not just a section of third party promotions, but actually an inherit functionality of Bolt app that gives drivers additional value for services that they need - exclusively for Bolt drivers. At least, this could be enabled for not high risk markets globally.

{quote}* _Displaying in-app banners in inboxes (i.e., a similar format to emails) would likely still count as ‘direct’ marketing._
* _Pop-up modals could be something to explore, as with in-app banners. We could also consider asking for ‘in-time’ consent (i.e., pop-ups asking for marketing consent when drivers visit the Bolt Rewards page) as a means of getting more users to consent to third-party marketing._
* _Push notifications would still be ‘direct’ marketing, but they are lower risk than emails. As such, if the business is desperate, we could explore these as well._
* {color:#4c9aff}*_Conclusion_*{color}_: Without third-party consent, we could use the following marketing mediums - (a) banners; (b) pop-up modals; and (if strictly needed) (c) push notifications. We can also deploy ‘in-time’ consent requests._{quote}

I agree with the overall conclusion. In general, we have informed marketing in the past that in-app banners and pop-ups are always possible without consent, so I am surprised to see this question here. Will clarify with Daria.

As a side note - any personalised banners/offers would be direct marketing, but the risk is so low we usually do not flag them as direct marketing to our teams.

{quote}* _On balance, particularly in higher-risk countries, this would still be interpreted as a promotional communication - the bottom line is that the purpose of the email is to promote Bolt Rewards. We could of course try and frame it in such a way as to present it as transactional, but if a regulator became interested I don’t think it would do us much good._
* _Nevertheless, admittedly, these comms would be lower risk than those directly encouraging drivers to sign up for Bolt Rewards (given that these ‘savings’ emails would be sent to drivers who are already benefitting from Bolt Rewards, and so they are less likely to complain)._
* {color:#4c9aff}*_Conclusion_*{color}_: These would still be marketing comms requiring consent. However, the risk profile is lower here, as drivers are unlikely to complain. As such, we could consider eating the risk if the business is desperate (although it is not something we should recommend in the first instance)._{quote}

I agree those would generally be seen as marketing; re/ risk, those are evidently not amount to essential service comms so I would generally see the risk as standard risk for marketing emails - I think I am a bit more conservative here than you:)

Likelihood of them being considered third party marketing is quite limited in my view - while the underlying purpose can be seen as promoting third party benefits, we are not promoting any party in particular, rather the idea of “Partner Offers” functionality in Bolt app.

Notes from a meeting on 03.11.2025 with merchant, billing, tax and product legal teams:

*Problem:* Currently with providers we override the data of the previous owner with data about new owner. So when we submit DAC7 report then we mix data about different owners and hence, report incorrect data where data is merged. Occurs when legal entity (i.e. owner) of the restaurant/merchant is changed - i.e. trademark stays the same on our platform, just legal entity behind that changes. 

Currently it is not realistical from technical perspective to rebuild the balances for the past and make sure that everything runs as DAC7 requires.

*Temporary solution*: What we have done so far in Croatia. We submit official letter for the partner which they can share with tax authority that we have reported incorrect data to tax authorities. The other option is that tax authority comes directly to us. 

Background: DAC7 enables tax authorities to collect info from platforms to make sure that partners using such platforms for selling their goods, have actually reported correct sums to tax authorities. They compare our data we report about the partner and the data partner reports. 

*Problems we have right now:*

# Partners are scared since tax authorities are after them. In reality if they did their books correctly they don’t have anything to be scared of. This is the place where us submitting the letter can help them to calm down. However, we should be careful not to give it to any partner and it also doesn’t mean that tax authority won’t take any actions against partner. This comes more visible issue with 2024 since more changes come apparent, main problems were 2023. 
# Tax authority can contact us directly and say why are mixing things up. Per market there might be different problems. 
# Partners won’t notify us on time when their ownership changed → wrong reporting + payments might go to wrong legal entity. 
# When merchant ownership changes then partner reaches out to AM or CS and then it goes to local market. Then they go to local market and change the owner name from old owner to new owner. In such case entity data is overridden - old and new entity data is mixed.

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


The refund is successfully completed. I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

[~accountid:712020:602d7a68-8a81-4bea-98bf-acb7026b1a56]  please find below my assessment!

*Executive Summary*

Under German taxi law (§ 39 Abs. 3 and § 51 Abs. 5 PBefG), the decisive legal requirement is that the taxi operator receives the full tariff amount for each trip. The Bundesgerichtshof (BGH, I ZR 34/17 – Bonusaktion für Taxi App) confirmed that passenger-side discounts or subsidies are lawful as long as the driver’s income equals the tariff and the discount is financed by a third party, not by the driver.

In the proposed setup, however, the 5 percent “booking fee” would be deducted from the driver’s gross fare. That means the driver no longer receives the full tariffed amount, which risks being seen as an unlawful tariff undercutting.

To remain compliant, the 5 percent must be treated as a separate post-tariff commission (similar to the already existing commission) for mediation or technical services, not as part of the tariff calculation. The technical setup must show that the full tariff price remains intact and that any platform fee is independent of the tariff system.

*Detailed Legal Assessment*

The taxi tariff obligation under § 39 Abs. 3 and § 51 Abs. 5 PBefG is designed to protect the integrity of the taxi market. What matters is that the taxi operator receives the full tariff amount set by the local ordinance. The Bundesgerichtshof clarified this in the decision I ZR 34/17 (Bonusaktion für Taxi App). The court held that the tariff rule is only breached when the taxi operator’s actual economic inflow is below the tariff, meaning when the driver ends up receiving less than the amount prescribed by the tariff.

The source of the payment is irrelevant. It makes no difference whether the passenger pays entirely out of pocket, pays less because of a discount, or whether a third party, such as an app platform, contributes to or subsidises the fare. The key legal point is that the taxi operator must still receive the full tariff amount for each trip.

This is why promotional discounts and rider incentives funded by a platform are lawful. The BGH even said explicitly that it does not matter whether the passenger finances the fare “aus eigenen Mitteln oder aus Mitteln unabhängiger Dritter.” In other words, what the passenger sees or pays is not a tariff problem, provided the driver receives the full tariffed price.

Where things get critical is when the platform takes part of that tariffed amount back from the driver. If a 5 percent “booking fee” is deducted from the gross tariff before the driver receives payment, the driver is no longer getting the full tariff. That creates the appearance of an impermissible undercutting of the tariffed fare. Even if the total amount paid by the passenger remains at the official tariff level, the legal test focuses on what the driver actually receives.

So the compliant structure is straightforward. The driver’s fare and receipt must correspond exactly to the tariff amount. Any rider discounts, reinvestments, or demand-side incentives must be paid from the platform’s own funds, not recouped through a reduction in the tariffed payout.

If the plan is to add a 5 percent “booking fee”, it should be defined contractually as a post-tariff commission for mediation services, not as part of the tariff composition itself. The technical setup should make clear that the tariff remains untouched and that the booking fee is a separate commercial arrangement between driver and platform. That approach should keep the scheme compliant with the PBefG and consistent with the reasoning of the BGH.

Relevant comments from [~accountid:612f31d89976c300693ebaf7] on [slack|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C09HFL73DPW], having reviewed input and the following documents provided by the compliance team:

* [+Extract from IFRS 15 Analysis+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gMBZpLx0QUz6K-zm1gqY-YxWMg3VKjnM/edit?usp=drive_link&ouid=100641143352541334136&rtpof=true&sd=true]
* [CZ and SK Ride-hailing T&C compliance review|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1YVx28iGdKJwjFlcFepRaab3yDyj8_nehNS-v6ZMjlnM/edit?tab=t.0]
* [+EY - Review of Terms and Conditions (2005)+|https://drive.google.com/file/d/18kOMGhbKEDNwWD4srBg5727HkukXrp3u/view]

+*Overview:*+

Compliance and legal are aligned; it's essential that Bolt positions itself as acting as an agent wherever possible. Some of our current practices, such as payment timing for service providers or incentives, may not fully align with that position, but we must still ensure that financial risk clearly sits with service providers, otherwise it can appear as though we’re employing them.

+*Scheduled rides:*+

{quote}[~accountid:63d0ecc7f386bda5dcab9d72]{color:#0747a6}_: Bolt accepts Rider bookings well in advance but only offers them to Drivers shortly before the ride. This means Bolt commits to fulfil the booking before securing a Driver, suggesting principal behaviour under IFRS 15. The risk is reinforced by marketing (e.g., “car will be waiting” for airport pick-ups), implying Bolt, not the Driver, makes the performance promise._{color}{quote}

Yes, this type of risk comes with offering scheduled rides, but it’s generally low. We can distinguish between ‘accepting a booking request’, which is what Bolt does, and ‘undertaking to perform the service’, which is what service providers do. Bolt doesn’t guarantee that any service will actually be performed. Many local transport regimes make this distinction explicitly, for example booking offices accept bookings while rides are fulfilled by licensed providers.

+*Late payment interest:*+

{quote}[~accountid:63d0ecc7f386bda5dcab9d72]{color:#0747a6}_: The T&Cs allow charging late interest, but this is not applied in practice. Consistent non-enforcement could create a constructive obligation or weaken Bolt’s position if challenged. This is not an issue from IFRS perspective, just highlighting that actual practise differs from T&Cs._{color}{quote}

Noted, and I agree that ongoing non-enforcement weakens enforceability. Clauses like this are really meant to cover significant non-payment of indemnities or legal damages, not minor account balance interest. There’s a good argument that it would be impractical for Bolt to recover such small amounts. If we were to recover interest in practice, we would issue a demand that formally crystallises the obligation to pay it.

+*Rider promotions:*+

{quote}[~accountid:63d0ecc7f386bda5dcab9d72]{color:#0747a6}_: The draft omits the previous clause stating that if a Passenger fare is discounted, Bolt compensates the Driver for the reduction. This creates uncertainty on who bears the cost of Rider promotions and may affect revenue recognition. For reference, previous versions of the T&Cs included this: “If the Fare paid by the Passengers is reduced as part of such campaign, we shall pay you compensation amounting to the monetary value of the benefit offered to the Passengers.”_{color}{quote}

This is intentional, as Bolt has no right to unilaterally discount 'the fare'. Doing so would align more with a principal or employment model. Instead, we should frame this as Bolt agreeing to cover part of the fare payable to drivers, though this raises broader tax and billing considerations. I've flagged to Tax that the way Bolt frames incentives should be reviewed in 2026 - compliance / accounting will be involved in this review.

+*Credit risk:*+

{quote}[~accountid:63d0ecc7f386bda5dcab9d72]{color:#0747a6}_: Although the T&Cs say Bolt pays Drivers only after collecting from Riders, in practice Bolt prepays Drivers. This exposes Bolt to Rider credit risk and, over time, could create a constructive obligation and support a view that Bolt acts as principal in substance._{color}{quote}

Yes, this is a known issue related to reclassification risk, and the business has been made aware of it many times. I don’t think there’s any appetite to change current practices yet, as Bolt doesn't want to deviate from competitor practices.

We asked Ilvestments to perform a BMS swap on two C2.5 batteries to evaluate the repairability of the battery and assess the repair quality.

In conclusion, 

* 1 out of the 2 BMS burned down during the process, 
* 42% of the solder joints do not meet the IPC-A-610 standard,
* battery was missing all BMS screws, which puts more mechanical stress on the solder joints. 

To improve the repair quality, we suggest that the repair partners train their technicians and ensures the use of proper tools and methods.
